positive: Many commenters are eager and counting down to pre-order, with some planning to order the moment sales open regardless of price.
Several name the configuration they want, most often white, unlocked, and high storage such as 512GB or more.
Some admit they don't really need it but are being won over by the design, feel, and uses like video viewing and reading.
Many commenters say they are excited and plan to buy or preorder the Duo as soon as it is released.
Some are drawn by the long-awaited foldable design and a large pocketable screen, and want it without leaving iOS.
Some accept missing features or weaker cameras, saying the novelty or their needs outweigh the drawbacks, while a few would rather wait for a later model.
negative: Many commenters say the price is far too high for a phone, and joke that buying it would drain their finances.
Several plan to wait for later versions or for evidence of screen durability, doubting a first-generation foldable will be reliable.
Some mock the name and the marketing of features, and say Apple fans will buy it regardless of its drawbacks.

positive: Most commenters say they plan to buy the phone anyway, so there are few real reasons against it here.
Perceived drawbacks such as Touch ID and no telephoto lens are dismissed as unimportant by fans who like the interface.
Cost is the main concern raised, though interest-free financing and bundled AppleCare offers are described as making the price manageable.
negative: Price is the main objection: commenters see the phone as far too expensive, especially in higher storage tiers once tax is added.
Some see it as a copycat of existing foldables, and say Android phones are the better choice for camera quality.
Features such as built-in MagSafe are seen as pointless or wasteful, since most people use a case anyway.

positive: Several commenters defend the high price as reasonable, seeing the device as worth the cost for its foldable design and for combining a phone with a larger screen.
Many say they are drawn by the folding design, smooth fold animations and software, and that they care less about camera strength.
Some find the phone appealing for specific uses such as reading documents, watching video and travelling light, though a few say they cannot afford it.
negative: Many commenters call the roughly $2,000 starting price excessive for a phone and say they would not pay it.
The entry model's storage and camera setup are seen as poor value at this price, and top configurations cost even more.
Some worry about costly repairs and long-term durability of the fold, and see the price as unjustified given possible flaws.

positive: Many commenters on older Pro or Pro Max models say they are upgrading to the Duo, calling it a fresh, more exciting change than another Pro.
Several say the Pro's camera matters little to them, citing past switches to the Air, and prefer the Duo unless they are serious photographers.
Some want the Duo to replace carrying a tablet or laptop for work and travel, or to offset cost with trade-ins.
negative: Many commenters say the Duo's price is too high, especially when a Pro Max costs less and already meets their needs.
Absence of Face ID, uncertainty about a first-generation product and little use for the inner display lead many to choose the Pro Max or wait for a later Duo.

positive: Many commenters who own a Samsung Fold say they are happy with it, praising its thinness, light weight and customisation, and plan to keep using it.
Several long-time Samsung users admit they are impressed by Apple's first foldable, though some argue Samsung remains innovative and that Apple is following its lead.

Some say Apple's ecosystem and polish could make its foldable stand out, and the price looks reasonable. One hopes the competition pushes Samsung to restore features like stylus support and water resistance.
negative: Many commenters say Apple is late to foldables and that Samsung has offered similar designs for years, so Apple's presentation feels overhyped.
Price is a frequent complaint: commenters think the Duo costs too much, in some places more than Samsung's Fold models, and should have top cameras.
Spec comparisons favor Samsung in places: the Duo is seen as heavier and lacking a fold durability rating, though some criticize Samsung's software and durability.

positive: Many commenters praise Apple's polished software, especially the fold and unfold transition and animations, calling it a distinctive Apple touch that sets it apart.
Several say they were not interested in foldables until Apple made one, and some waited for it, preferring iOS and its simplicity over better-specced Android options.
Some say Apple is impressive for a first foldable and trusted for build quality, while a few note that rivals copy each other or that Android already offers multitasking.
negative: Many commenters say Apple copies Android and Samsung features, arriving late with few original ideas and little real innovation.
Apple fans are accused of hypocrisy: they mocked foldables as gimmicks before, but now praise them because Apple is making one.
Some criticise Apple's pricing and first-generation products, expecting high costs, early flaws and a quick successor, though a few concede Apple's appeal.

positive: Many praise the matte inner screen, saying it looks attractive, helps hide the crease, and suits long reading sessions.
The transition between the outer and inner screens when folding or unfolding is described as smooth, clean and polished.
Commenters like having a bigger screen in a pocket, with better multitasking and larger text, and see the display as a real upgrade.
negative: Many dislike the inner screen's matte, anti-reflective finish, seeing it as a way to hide the crease, and they dislike the curved edges.
Commenters worry about durability and repair cost: foldable screens failing within about a year, expensive replacements, accessories, and possible AppleCare deductibles.
The smaller outer screen and the modestly larger inner display draw criticism: less sharp, awkward for left-handed users, and not worth the price.

positive: Commenters prefer a hidden under-display camera to a hole punch or notch, valuing an uninterrupted, clean full screen on the inner display.
Many say selfies would mostly use the outer display camera anyway, so any quality tradeoff in the inner camera matters little.
The matte inner display gets praise for hiding the crease and looking and feeling good, and some expect rivals to improve the technology.
negative: Several commenters say under-display cameras were abandoned because of poor image quality, so they are skeptical of the idea returning.
Some find the inner screen grainy or inaccurate in colour, and they dislike the matte finish and visible fingerprint smudges.
Others care little about selfies and put more weight on other issues, such as camera bumps, the number of rear lenses, or screen durability.

positive: Commenters widely praise the open and close transition as smooth, clean and seamless, with many calling it clever or genius and saying the designers deserve credit.
The blur and see-through effect on the outer panel is noted as creating a convincing illusion, and some say it shows Apple's knack for simple, sensible ideas.
Several believe the animation alone could drive sales, and even fans of rival foldables admit it is impressive and addictive to repeat.
negative: Commenters think it's underwhelming that a fold or unfold animation is treated as the phone's standout feature after so many years.
Some say the effect is just a basic blur transition and not impressive.
One viewer noted the screen animation glitched when the phone was closed.

positive: Many left-handed commenters say they already hold phones in their right hand or have adapted to right-handed devices, so it isn't a dealbreaker.
Some right-handed users say they mostly operate their phone with the left hand, so they see the handedness concern as minor.
A few expect a software setting could mirror or rotate the interface for left-handed users, and think the worry is overblown.
negative: Left-handed users say the Duo's layout seems built for right-handed use, so they expect it to be awkward or frustrating.
Several commenters worry that Face ID placement would make unlocking the phone difficult when it is held in the left hand.
Some feel left-handed people were overlooked, and they mock the idea that they should just hold the phone differently or switch hands.

positive: Apple Pencil support is a major selling point for several commenters, who see it as a deciding reason to buy the Duo.
Many want to use the larger inner screen for sketching, painting and productivity, treating the phone like a mini iPad.
Some users of rival foldables say the lack of pen support on those devices makes the Duo's compatibility feel like a clear advantage.
Many commenters see the device as a combined phone and iPad mini, and some say they would replace both devices with one.
Fans praise the folding form factor and software, including the side toolbar, button placement and flexible orientations, and suggest uses like reading, navigation, medical work and retro gaming.
Several say they don't mind the camera trade-offs because they mostly use the phone for browsing and media, or use a separate camera.
negative: Many see the foldable as essentially a small iPad in phone form, so they question its point and say a regular iPad would do.
The high price draws repeated criticism: commenters say it costs more than an iPad and isn't worth it for what it offers.
Some doubt the design and practicality, citing a visible crease, awkward width when folded, and the large screen being used less than expected.

positive: Many commenters are excited about the foldable design, calling it the most interesting iPhone in years and a refreshing change from the standard look.
Several say they plan to buy it or switch to it, including long-time Apple users and some Android users.
Some like the build and display details, such as a durable titanium body, an invisible front camera, slim bezels and a wish for tougher glass.
negative: Commenters say the foldable is very heavy, and adding a case would make one-handed use difficult.
Some joke that Apple made it heavy on purpose so later models can be advertised as lighter or with a less visible crease.
Several see the design as copying Google and Samsung foldables, and some say a flip style would have suited Apple better.

positive: Many commenters are very excited and plan to preorder or buy the Duo, often saying the desire comes first and justifications follow.
Viewers like the book-like opening, the hardware and software integration, and the way the design reduces the visibility of the fold crease.
People expect the device to suit reading, video and side-by-side scrolling, and hope features like the hidden selfie camera carry into future models.
negative: Commenters think the Duo is too expensive, with high regional prices and storage tiers, and heavy for a foldable. Some say rivals offer more for the price.
Many doubt demand for a foldable iPhone, criticising a weaker camera setup, thick and heavy build, unproven durability, and unclear specs such as battery capacity.
Practical worries include case choice, an uneven camera bump on flat surfaces, typing with two apps open, carrier lock-ins, and disputed chip performance claims.

positive: Commenters expect strong developer support, with apps being adapted for the dual-screen design, and think this could also improve iPad versions of those apps.
Software transitions and the polished app experience get praise, with some saying they've changed their view of foldables and make the device more appealing.
Running two apps side by side is seen as a sensible, sufficient level of multitasking, and the device is liked for reading.
negative: Commenters doubt the foldable's multitasking value, saying features like dragging apps into different view modes feel borrowed from iPad software and add little for real use.
Several say multitasking in portrait seems limited to things like pop-up video, so it looks more like marketing hype than a useful feature.
Some complain about hardware choices, such as the action button replacing the mute switch and the odd placement of volume buttons, and about the very high price.

positive: Some commenters prefer a fingerprint sensor, calling it faster and more convenient than Face ID, and not needing an Apple Watch to unlock.
A few feel more comfortable with fingerprint unlocking because it avoids the sense of constant face scanning and privacy worries.
Others praise the device's polished, high-tech look and say it makes them more interested in buying one.
negative: Lacking Face ID is treated as a serious drawback, and at least one viewer is waiting for a later model because of it.
Wider complaints say the device is not innovative, borrows heavily from rival foldables, and is priced too high for what it offers.
Some commenters also criticise the software layout, citing wasted screen space in landscape mode and an oversized keyboard.

positive: Many commenters see the device as polished and exciting for a first-generation foldable, and several say they plan to buy it.
Some defend its missing features as normal for a first model, arguing that leaving room for later upgrades keeps people interested.
A few note that earlier foldable makers, such as Motorola, came first, and some say the crease is barely visible.
negative: Commenters mock Apple's foldable as late and not truly innovative, since rival brands have offered foldable phones for years.
Some worry about durability, especially a crease that grows more visible over time, as on earlier foldables they owned.
Others suspect Apple manipulates expectations through leaks about price and low supply, and see the short return window as a risk.
